questions.q: State the three cases for consistency of a system AX = B with square matrix A, giving the condition on |A| and (adj A)B for each case.
questions.a: Case 1: |A| ≠ 0 → unique solution (consistent). Case 2: |A| = 0 and (adj A)B ≠ 0 → no solution (inconsistent). Case 3: |A| = 0 and (adj A)B = 0 → may be consistent (infinitely many solutions) or inconsistent (no solution); further check needed. A wrong answer (e.g., saying Case 3 is always consistent) reveals the student has memorized the first two cases but not the nuance of the third case, which is a common JEE trap.

questions.q: For the system x + 2y = 3 and 2x + 4y = 7, write the matrix form AX = B, compute |A| and (adj A)B, and state whether the system is consistent or inconsistent. Explain why the result makes sense geometrically.
questions.a: A = [[1, 2], [2, 4]], B = [3, 7]ᵀ. |A| = 1·4 – 2·2 = 0. adj A = [[4, -2], [-2, 1]]. (adj A)B = [4·3 + (-2)·7, (-2)·3 + 1·7]ᵀ = [12–14, -6+7]ᵀ = [-2, 1]ᵀ ≠ 0. Hence inconsistent. Geometrically, the two lines are parallel (slopes both -1/2) but have different intercepts, so they never intersect. A student who only checks |A| = 0 and concludes "infinitely many solutions" misses the (adj A)B check and makes the classic error of confusing dependent and inconsistent systems.

questions.q: Determine the consistency of the system: 2x – y + 3z = 5, 4x – 2y + 6z = 10, 6x – 3y + 9z = 15. Show all steps including computation of |A| and (adj A)B.
questions.a: A = [[2, -1, 3], [4, -2, 6], [6, -3, 9]], B = [5, 10, 15]ᵀ. Notice R2 = 2R1, R3 = 3R1 → rows are proportional → |A| = 0. Compute adj A: all cofactors will be zero because every 2×2 minor has proportional rows → adj A = zero matrix. Then (adj A)B = 0. Since |A| = 0 and (adj A)B = 0, the system may be consistent. Check proportionality of full equations: second equation is 2× first, third is 3× first → all three represent the same plane → infinitely many solutions (consistent). A wrong answer claiming "inconsistent because |A|=0" shows failure to compute (adj A)B and check equation proportionality.

questions.q: Compare the consistency conditions for a 2×2 system and a 3×3 system. Are the criteria exactly the same? If a 3×3 system has |A| = 0 and (adj A)B = 0, what additional step is required to decide between infinitely many solutions and no solution?
questions.a: The criteria are identical in form: |A| ≠ 0 → unique; |A| = 0, (adj A)B ≠ 0 → inconsistent; |A| = 0, (adj A)B = 0 → ambiguous. For 3×3, when (adj A)B = 0, we must check whether the equations are linearly dependent (one is a linear combination of others) by comparing ratios of coefficients and constants. If all equations are proportional (or one is a combination of others with matching constants), infinitely many solutions; otherwise, no solution. A student who says "the criteria are exactly the same for all n" misses the practical need for row reduction or proportionality check in the ambiguous case for n≥3.

questions.q: A student solves the system x + y + z = 6, 2x + 2y + 2z = 12, 3x + 3y + 3z = 18 and writes: "|A| = 0, so the system has no solution." Evaluate this statement and correct the error.
questions.a: The statement is false. |A| = 0 only tells us the system does NOT have a unique solution; it could have infinitely many or N/A. Here, second equation = 2×first, third = 3×first, and constants match the same multiples → (adj A)B = 0 and equations are proportional → infinitely many solutions (consistent). The student confused |A| = 0 with inconsistency. The correct conclusion: consistent with infinitely many solutions (a plane of solutions).

questions.q: Construct a 3×3 system of linear equations that has |A| = 0 and (adj A)B = 0 but is INCONSISTENT. Explain why your example works.
questions.a: Example: x + y + z = 1, 2x + 2y + 2z = 2, 3x + 3y + 3z = 5. A = [[1,1,1],[2,2,2],[3,3,3]], B = [1,2,5]ᵀ. |A| = 0 (rows proportional). adj A = 0 matrix (all minors have proportional rows) → (adj A)B = 0. But third equation is 3×first equation on LHS (3x+3y+3z) while RHS is 5 ≠ 3×1 = 3 → contradiction. Hence no solution. This works because (adj A)B = 0 is necessary but not sufficient for consistency when |A| = 0; the constants must also satisfy the same linear relations as the coefficients.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: A system of linear equations AX = B is consistent if at least one solution exists (unique or infinitely many); it is ______ if no solution exists.
Fill in the blank: Imagine you are a shopkeeper in Delhi who sells three items: apples (₹x/kg), ______ (₹y/kg), and oranges (₹z/kg).

Fill in the blank: If |A| = ______, you must check (adj A)B — if non-zero, the customers' bills contradict each other (inconsistent); if zero, the bills might be redundant (infinitely many price combinations) or still contradictory.
What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: Student can: (1) write the matrix form AX = B for any given system of 2 or 3 linear equations, (2) compute |A| and classify the system as having a unique solution, no solution, or infinitely many solutions, (3) correctly compute (adj A)B when |A| = 0 and interpret the result, (4) distinguish between the three cases using the criteria.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Imagine you are a ______ in Delhi who sells three items: apples (₹x/kg), bananas (₹y/kg), and oranges (₹z/kg).
